references.title: The Four Steps to the Epiphany
references.summary: Customer development: customer discovery, customer validation, customer creation, company building. Discovery and validation search for a repeatable business model; creation and building execute it.

stance.why: Discovery and Validation take Blank's names and meaning.

references.title: Crossing the Chasm
references.summary: The technology adoption life cycle and the chasm between visionaries and pragmatists; cross it by winning one beachhead segment, then neighbouring niches (the bowling alley).

stance.why: Beachhead keeps Moore's meaning: one mainstream segment won outright.

references.title: Inside the Tornado
references.summary: Companion to Crossing the Chasm: the tornado of mass-market adoption and Main Street after it.

stance.why: Scale covers the tornado and Main Street under the common word.

references.title: The only thing that matters (Pmarca Guide to Startups, part 4)
references.summary: Product/market fit means being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market; credits Andy Rachleff. The original blog was taken down and survives on an archive.

stance.why: The Validation gate is product-market fit, tested by retention.

references.title: Repeatability: Build Enduring Businesses for a World of Constant Change
references.summary: Bain study of 200+ companies: enduring growth comes from a repeatable business model; complexity is a silent killer of profitable growth.

references.title: The Alchemy of Growth
references.summary: McKinsey's three horizons: H1 extend the core, H2 build emerging businesses, H3 create options. The horizons run at the same time, as a portfolio.

stance.why: Used as a lens, not as phase names, because its horizons are concurrent rather than sequential.

references.title: Expanded six-phase milestone framework (Discovery, Validation, Retention, Repeatability, Scale, Platformization)
authors: Google (AI assistant conversation shared by the founder)
references.summary: A synthesized six-phase model separating retention (product-market fit) and repeatability from validation and scale. No published source.

stance.why: Retention and repeatability became gates rather than phases; Platformization became Platform.

references.title: The thin edge of the wedge strategy
references.summary: Enter a market with a narrow product or segment that solves an acute problem, then expand from that foothold; related to the bowling-pin strategy.

stance.why: Wedge is a portfolio role with this meaning, not a phase.

references.title: Defining the Business: The Starting Point of Strategic Planning
references.summary: A business is defined on three dimensions: customer groups (who), customer functions (what need), and technologies (how).

stance.why: Market, job and technology on each product card.

references.title: North American Industry Classification System 2022
references.summary: Production-oriented industry classification: 20 sectors, six-digit codes; establishments with similar production processes share an industry.

references.title: Global Industry Classification Standard
references.summary: Market-oriented industry classification used by investors.

stance.why: Kept as an alternative system; NAICS is the default.

references.title: Treasury Regulation 1.183-2: activity not engaged in for profit
references.summary: Nine factors for whether an activity is a business or a hobby; an activity profitable in 3 of 5 years is presumed for profit.

stance.why: hobby is the first value of ambition, in the IRS sense.

references.title: What Do Entrepreneurs Create?
references.summary: Four venture types: survival, lifestyle, managed growth, aggressive growth; ventures rarely change type, and a portfolio should balance types.

references.title: The Business Model Navigator
references.summary: 55 recurring business model patterns from the University of St. Gallen; a business model answers who, what, how and how revenue is realized.

stance.why: business_model values are the Navigator's pattern names.

references.title: The Core Competence of the Corporation
references.summary: A core competence is collective learning that gives access to many markets, adds to perceived customer benefit and is hard to imitate; core products embody it.

references.title: Principles of Marketing: the three levels of product
references.summary: A product has levels: the core customer benefit, the actual product, and the augmented product.

stance.why: The core promise is the core benefit stated as what anyone can claim from the venture.
